summary: This standards-track RFC describes a YANG library listing all YANG modules used by a network management server, such as a NETCONF server. It provides simple caching so clients can avoid re-fetching the information. It was replaced by RFC 8525.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents telling a client which data models a device supports. This version was replaced by RFC 8525.

questions: how to list yang modules on a netconf server
subtitle: A standard way for clients to discover which YANG data models a network device supports.

tldr.problem: Network management clients need to know which YANG modules (data models) a server supports, but there was no standard way to get this information. Without caching, clients had to repeatedly fetch a potentially large list of modules.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a YANG library data structure that lists all modules on a server, includes a change identifier so clients can cache the list and only refetch it when the identifier changes.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now discover server capabilities once and reuse that information, reducing bandwidth and latency. RFC 8525 later replaced this with an improved version.

today: RFC 8525 supersedes this RFC with YANG Library 2.0, which provides additional capabilities and improved semantics.

sections.title: What Is a YANG Library
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to describe the configuration and state data of network devices. A large network device might implement hundreds of YANG modules, each describing a different feature or subsystem. When a client connects to a device via a management protocol like NETCONF, it needs to understand which modules the device supports and which features of those modules are enabled.

The YANG library is a standardized data structure that a server publishes to tell clients exactly which YANG modules and submodules it supports, what revisions are in use, what optional features are enabled, and which deviation statements have been applied. This information is essential for clients to correctly interpret the configuration and state data they retrieve from the server.
sections.plainLanguage: A server supports many different data models (YANG modules). The library is just a list that says "I support module X version 1.5, module Y version 2.0, and for module X I have features A and B turned on."

sections.title: Caching with Module Set Identifiers
sections.content:
The YANG library includes a module-set-id, a unique identifier that represents the current set of modules and submodules supported by the server. Whenever the set of modules changes—for example, if a new feature is loaded or an old module is unloaded—the server generates a new module-set-id value.

Clients can fetch the YANG library once, cache the module list, and store the module-set-id. On subsequent connections, the client queries only the module-set-id value. If it matches the cached value, the module list has not changed. If it is different, the client refetches the full list. This caching mechanism is especially important for servers with hundreds of modules, where transmitting the full list every time would be expensive.

When the module-set-id changes, the server also sends a notification (if notifications are enabled) to inform any connected clients that the module list has been updated. For NETCONF servers implementing YANG 1.1, this change also affects the NETCONF server capabilities advertised in the server hello message.
sections.plainLanguage: The server assigns a number to its module list. If the number changes, the list changed; if not, it is the same. Clients keep the old list cached and only download a new one when the number changes.

sections.title: Module List Structure
sections.content:
The YANG library data is provided by the ietf-yang-library YANG module, which defines a read-only container called modules-state. For each module, the library records the module name, the revision date (in YYYY-MM-DD format), the XML namespace, the list of supported features, the list of used deviation modules, and the conformance type (either "implement" or "import").

A module with conformance type "implement" means the server actually implements the protocol-accessible objects from that module. A conformance type "import" means the server imports definitions from the module (for reuse) but does not implement any protocol-accessible objects from it. The library also lists all submodules used by each module, with their names and revisions.
sections.plainLanguage: For each module, the list says its name, date, features turned on, which other modules it uses, and whether the server actually uses it or just borrowed some definitions from it.

sections.title: Accessing the YANG Library
sections.content:
Clients retrieve the YANG library via the standard NETCONF get operation (or equivalent management protocol operations). Since the library is read-only state data, it cannot be configured. The server maintains it automatically based on its current module configuration.

The library information can differ on each server and can change at runtime if the server loads or unloads modules. If a server implements multiple management protocols (such as NETCONF and RESTCONF), each protocol has its own conceptual instantiation of the YANG library, though they typically reflect the same underlying module set.

Clients can also subscribe to the yang-library-change notification to be alerted whenever the module-set-id changes, eliminating the need to periodically poll the server for updates.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to a server, you ask for the module list. The server tells you. If you connect again later and the number hasn't changed, you use your old copy. If it changed, you ask again.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The YANG library is read-only state data. Because it reveals which modules and features are available on a server, it may be sensitive in some network environments. Some system operators might not want to advertise their configuration capabilities to all clients. Access control to the YANG library should be configured according to the NETCONF access control model defined in RFC 6536 or equivalent controls in other management protocols.

The YANG library itself does not contain sensitive data like configuration values or statistics; it only describes the structure and capabilities of the data model. However, a hostile client could use the library information to target attacks against specific modules or features known to be enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of modules is read-only and mostly harmless, but knowing what a server supports helps an attacker pick a target. Network administrators might want to restrict who can see the list.
